name: Jonafree

origin.place: PRI co-operative breeding programme (Purdue, Rutgers and Illinois universities), USA
origin.parentage: Complex (PRI 855-102 x NJ 31); ancestry includes Crandall's Rome x Malus floribunda 821, Jonathan, Gallia Beauty, Red Spy and Golden Delicious

history: A scab-resistant apple from the PRI co-operative programme, which bred the floribunda scab-resistance gene into dessert apples. It was selected in the 1960s and released in 1979 as Co-op 22.

look.description: Medium, rounded fruit almost entirely covered with a bright red flush.

taste.summary: Crisp, juicy flesh with a Jonathan-style flavour but noticeably less acid than Jonathan.

pollination.notes: Early-flowering: Orange Pippin lists group 1 and National Fruit Collection dates are among the earliest; group 2 used as a compromise.

climate.best_climates: Humid eastern and midwestern US climates where scab pressure is high and a spray-free apple is wanted.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust, to which it is susceptible.

health.other: Carries the Vf scab-resistance gene; rated susceptible to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials.

grow_notes: Good for low-spray gardens because of its scab resistance, but keep it away from junipers where cedar-apple rust occurs. Needs an early-flowering pollinator.

name: Jonamac

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.raised_by: Roger D. Way, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

history: Raised in 1944 by Roger Way at Geneva, New York, and introduced in 1972. It combines McIntosh's white flesh with some of Jonathan's richer flavour, and is itself a parent of the Canadian apple Eden.

look.description: Medium, round fruit largely covered with bright red flush and stripes over pale yellow.

taste.summary: Very white, moderately firm flesh with a McIntosh-type aromatic flavour, sweeter and improved by the Jonathan parent. Orange Pippin also lists honeyed and strawberry notes.

tree.notes: Good cropper with some tendency to alternate bearing; fruit hangs well on the tree.

climate.best_climates: Cool, cold-winter regions such as New York, New England and eastern Canada, like its McIntosh parent.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers, where McIntosh-type apples go soft and colour poorly.

health.other: Some scab susceptibility; some resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

grow_notes: A hardy early-autumn apple for cold districts. Thin the fruit in heavy years to reduce alternate cropping, and use the fruit within a few weeks.

name: Julyred

origin.place: New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, New Brunswick, New Jersey, USA
origin.parentage: (Petrel x Early McIntosh) x (Williams x Starr)
origin.raised_by: G. W. Schneider, New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

history: An early summer apple from the New Jersey breeding programme, introduced in 1962. It is a parent of Jerseymac and appears in the pedigrees of several later New Jersey apples.

look.description: Large, attractive, rounded fruit, striped and flushed red over pale green.

taste.summary: Soft, white, juicy flesh with a strongly scented, wine-like flavour likened to loganberry. A sweet summer apple to eat straight from the tree.
taste.best_eaten: Aug; within a week of picking

climate.best_climates: Mid-Atlantic and north-eastern US climates, where it provides fruit in July.
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure.

health.other: Rated susceptible to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials; otherwise not well recorded.

grow_notes: Pick over several passes as fruits colour and eat promptly; like most summer apples it goes soft within a week or so.

name: Keepsake

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota, USA

history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1978 as a very hardy, long-keeping winter apple. Its homely, irregular looks kept it out of supermarkets, but it found fame as a parent of Honeycrisp.

look.description: Small to medium, lumpy and irregular fruit, mostly covered with red flush and streaks.

taste.summary: Very hard, crisp, fine-grained and juicy light-yellow flesh with a strongly aromatic, sweet and spicy flavour. It mellows in store and is at its best in mid-winter.
taste.best_eaten: Dec-Mar; peaks in Jan-Feb after storage

tree.notes: Medium vigour and easy to manage; comes into bearing early but tends to crop biennially.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates such as Minnesota and the northern US and Canada, where it is very hardy.
climate.poor_climates: Short-season districts where it cannot be left to mid-October; untested in hot climates.

health.other: Good general disease resistance; some resistance to fire blight and cedar-apple rust.

grow_notes: Pick late and store cool; it needs two or three months in store to reach full flavour. Thin in heavy years to curb biennial cropping.

name: Lakeland

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota, USA

history: One of the University of Minnesota's mid-century hardy apples, introduced in 1950 from a Malinda seedling. A general-purpose apple for cold northern gardens.

look.description: Medium to large, broadly conical fruit, flushed and streaked dark purplish red over yellowish green, with a waxy skin.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, juicy cream to yellow flesh, sometimes tinged red, with a sweet and mildly acid flavour. A good all-round apple for eating, pies and sauce.

climate.best_climates: Cold-winter northern climates such as Minnesota, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; hardy northern apples generally do less well in hot summers.

health.other: Disease behaviour not recorded in the sources used.

grow_notes: Mainly of interest for very cold gardens. Use early fruit for cooking and let the rest store until December.

name: Merton Delight

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, London, England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Golden Pippin (National Fruit Collection); Orange Pippin gives Cox's Orange Pippin x Golden Russet
origin.raised_by: M. B. Crane, John Innes Institution

history: One of the Merton seedlings raised by M. B. Crane at the John Innes Institution in the 1930s from a Cox cross. It was not taken up commercially and was dropped from British trials in 1959.

look.description: Medium, flattish yellow fruit with pinkish-red stripes.

taste.summary: Tender, crisp, creamy flesh with a sweet to gently acid flavour.

pollination.notes: No published group found; estimated from National Fruit Collection flowering dates and its Cox parentage.

climate.best_climates: Southern English conditions, where it was raised and trialled.

grow_notes: A rare collection apple; grow as for Cox, with a group 3 partner and a sheltered site.

name: Milton

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York, USA
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

history: Crossed in 1909 by Richard Wellington at Geneva and introduced in 1923 by the New York State Fruit Testing Association. An early-autumn McIntosh-type apple.

look.description: Medium, ribbed, conical fruit, pale yellow largely covered by a deep cherry-red flush.

taste.summary: Soft, fine and very white flesh, juicy and sweet with low acidity and a hint of raspberry.

pollination.notes: Group 2 per Orange Pippin; early-flowering at Brogdale.

climate.best_climates: Cool north-eastern US and Canadian climates suited to its McIntosh and Yellow Transparent parents.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; soft early fruit is unlikely to stand hot weather.

health.other: Rated very resistant to cedar-apple rust in Arkansas trials; other diseases not recorded.

grow_notes: Eat soon after picking. Pair with another early-flowering apple for pollination.

name: Mio

origin.raised_by: Emil Johansson, Alnarp horticultural research station

history: Crossed in 1932 at Alnarp in southern Sweden and sold from 1956; named after Astrid Lindgren's children's book 'Mio, min Mio'. A popular early-autumn garden apple in Sweden.

look.description: Medium to large, ribbed, conical fruit, mostly red-striped over a pale green ground; skin becomes greasy.

taste.summary: Soft, white flesh tinged with pink, sweet with a light acidity. The National Fruit Collection found the flavour rather insipid in Kent.

pollination.notes: Swedish sources call it medium-early flowering and list James Grieve, Katja, Melba and Transparente Blanche among good partners.

climate.best_climates: Southern and central Sweden (Swedish zones I-IV) and similar cool northern climates.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; in the milder, warmer English climate its flavour was judged dull.

health.other: Good scab resistance reported in Sweden.

grow_notes: A garden apple for cool northern climates; pick in early September and use promptly.
